name: Antigua and Barbuda
rule: Supported by a combined domestic-category and commodity-classification inference for the stated manufactured plain tea. The PPU’s 27 August 2020 all-country commodity table applies permit/phytosanitary requirements to Categories 2–4. Its signed 17 June 2021 guidance and current website require documents for regulated plant commodities and describe processed items that still carry pests; the PPU expressly operates within IPPC standards. Current-linked ISPM 32 section 2 and Appendix 2 identify tea as a Category 1 example. This is a reasoned application of the domestic scheme, not a freestanding international exemption. A broad older leaflet requiring certificates for non-regulated items was recovered in an IPPC report dated 14 May 2014; the ministry copy uploaded in 2022 changes only its contact email. Newer signed/current guidance supplies the operative narrower scope. Separate enacted food laws reviewed do not impose a blanket private-tea origin certificate.
personalMailApplicability: Product-scope inference applies to a clean sealed 100 g manufactured Camellia tea packet bought for personal use and sent by post; it is not a traveler or gift allowance. Ordinary customs declaration and arrival inspection remain.
authority: Antigua and Barbuda Plant Protection Unit
researchAttempts: Reviewed PPU import guidance and the 27 August 2020 commodity-status table, including processed-food examples. No explicit heat-processed Camellia tea classification or small postal waiver found.

2026-09-30: Re-read the current official PPU page in the browser. It regulates any quantity only when the article is regulated; processing examples include crushed herbs, dehydrated fruit/vegetables and other pest-bearing preparations, but do not classify steamed manufactured Camellia tea. Public generic processing guidance is exhausted without that commodity determination.

2026-09-30: Downloaded and read the complete 10-page official commodity-status table dated 27 August 2020. The all-country row specifically addresses Categories 2–4 and requires permit plus phytosanitary certificate; no Camellia tea/Japan entry or Category 1 processing determination appears. Rechecked current PPU guidance and targeted cooking/steaming/sterilisation/Category 1 guidance. No published product determination found; did not infer either automatic exemption or a Japan-origin ban.

Read official Public Health Act Cap. 353, Part VI: section 49 defines food and importer broadly; section 57(1)(a) authorizes food-import regulations for food intended for sale; section 66(e) enforces applicable food-import regulations; section 67 permits sampling of imported consignments. These provisions do not themselves create a blanket origin/free-sale/health-certificate requirement for private tea imports.

Read official Importation Protection Act Cap. 211 sections 3–6: section 3 authorizes controls for imported articles intended for sale and contains a rebuttable sale presumption. The express origin-health-certificate duty in section 4 applies to secondhand clothing, not tea. The traveller personal-effects exception in section 6 likewise concerns clothing, so it was not used as a food exemption.

Searched official legislation, ministry health guidance, food-import requirements and free-sale certificate terms. The located Food Safety Act 2017 file is in the Bills collection and the ministry labels its 2020 text Food Safety Bill; neither was treated as an enacted private-import obligation. No separate enacted blanket food-certificate or import-approval rule was established. The existing plant-risk classification gap therefore remains unresolved.

30 September bounded legal-scope peer review: The operative public guidance consistently limits permits and certificates to regulated commodities. The complete table addresses Categories 2–4; it is not a complete list of exempt Category 1 goods. Its examples include crushed herbs, dehydrated fruit/vegetables, and even a steam/pressure-treated tamarind commodity. These demonstrate that either being processed or having a heat treatment in the name does not automatically prove exemption. No table entry or local processing definition settles steamed/dried Camellia tea. Japan omission cannot itself be treated as a ban outside the regulated scope.

Fresh official media-index recovery found the 17 June 2021 signed Plant Protection Importation Guidelines and the apparently newer /2022/06/ import-export guide. Recovered the same broad guide from an IPPC national report published/updated 14 May 2014. Comparing normalized full texts shows the only change is the contact email domain; the 2022 upload is not evidence of a newly issued broader rule. Older guide requires certificates even for non-regulated items, while newer signed guidance/current PPU website expressly say regulated plant commodities.

Recovered and read the complete enacted Plant Protection Act 18/2012 from the national repository and searchable FAO mirror. Section 2 defines manufactured plant products by pest risk; section 15(2) allows NPPO requirements for certain covered articles, and section 16(2) uses international standards/risk analysis. No unqualified statutory certificate duty for every food or non-regulated plant-origin item was found.

Current PPU page expressly states that the agency operates within ISPMs. Re-read the complete 27 August 2020 domestic status table: all-country permit/certificate controls address Categories 2–4. Current-linked ISPM 32 section 2 and Appendix 2 (printed page 32-18) now supply the missing commodity evidence by listing tea as a Category 1 example. The Appendix is reference-only, not itself prescriptive; support is a combined-source domestic-scope inference for manufactured sencha rather than a universal processing exemption.

Rechecked the current Ministry of Health Laws & Regulations index online: it still labels the Food Safety text as Food Safety Bill 2020. Re-read saved enacted Public Health Act sections 57/66 and Importation Protection Act sections 3–6: food-import regulation powers and sale scope do not themselves create an unqualified personal-tea foreign certificate duty; the express certificate provision concerns used clothing. No separate mandatory special food document was established for this private packet.
permitFreeReason: No special documents supported for the stated manufactured tea on a combined-source inference: the local commodity schedule regulates Categories 2–4, current/signed PPU guidance limits documents to regulated goods, and the current-linked ISPM 32 illustration places tea in Category 1. Plant Protection Act 2012 section 2 is risk-qualified for manufactured products, consistent with this reading. Appendix 2 is illustrative/non-prescriptive and is not used alone to override local law. The 2014 broad leaflet is disclosed but weighed against the newer 2021/current PPU scope.
paperworkType: None identified for stated personal manufactured-tea parcel on combined-source interpretation; ordinary customs declaration and inspection remain.
requiredDocument: Ordinary postal/customs declaration only under the reviewed rules; no plant permit, phytosanitary certificate or blanket private-food origin certificate on the stated interpretation.

name: Suriname
rule: Supported by a combined statutory and commodity-classification inference for sealed manufactured plain Camellia tea. Plantenbeschermingswet 2020 article 1(1)(bb) includes manufactured products only when their nature/processing creates pest risk, and article 1(2) expressly gives IPPC/SPS term meanings and associated standards/guidelines priority. Current-linked ISPM 32 section 2 treats Category 1 commodities as requiring no phytosanitary measures; Appendix 2 expressly illustrates tea in Category 1. The Appendix is reference-only, not a freestanding binding exemption, but supplies the missing commodity evidence when applying the domestic definition. Articles 5–8/14 and the August 2026 notice control covered plants/products; neither specifically reclassifies manufactured tea. The separate trade Negative List omits tea and no enacted private-food certificate requirement was established.
personalMailApplicability: The interpretation concerns the product’s exclusion from regulated plant-product scope and is not limited to passenger baggage or gifts. It therefore applies to the stated 100 g paid private postal purchase, subject to ordinary customs declarations, inspection and clean manufactured retail packaging.
authority: Suriname Ministry of Agriculture, Livestock and Fisheries NPPO
researchAttempts: Read and OCRed the 14 August 2026 official import procedure notice, then compared the 2023 government explanation of plant-product scope. The finished-tea classification remains unresolved.

2026-09-30: Checked current Parliament record: Levensmiddelenwet 2026 submitted 6 March 2026 remains under pending bills with adoption date blank; did not apply its draft controls. Read the IUD ministry import guidance, full original 2003 Negative List (FAOLEX copy of official Gazette, including import annex) and OCR-read the government’s 2006 amendment. The plant-certification annex enumerates chapters 6, 7, 8, 10, 12 and 25, not 9; it supplies no general all-food origin-certificate category. The 2006 amendment concerns chemicals/ozone products and metal exports. Business-licensing conditions and trade-business registration guidance were not applied to private postal tea. Without a current NPPO finished-tea classification or complete current overriding exemption, preserved unresolved rather than assuming old schedule omission establishes present permission.

30 September bounded independent peer review: retrieved the complete enacted Plantenbeschermingswet 2020, S.B. 2020 no.78, from Parliament and reread the actual official 2023 LVV newsletter. Article 1(1)(bb), printed p.4, expressly includes pest-risk-bearing processed products; the newsletter pp.3–4 is a simplified explanation and cannot establish a manufactured-food exemption. Read articles 1(2), 2(5)–(6), 5–8 and 14: IPPC/SPS term meanings take priority, but this clause does not itself classify sencha or incorporate a commodity-specific no-document route. Article 6(3) removes the phytosanitary certificate only for processed frozen fruit/vegetables and still requires permission. Article 14 expressly includes postal custody of unauthorised covered goods. No published list in this Act supplies a tea classification; its regime is independent of the older trade Negative List. Preserved unresolved and saved the enacted PDF/text plus newsletter at caribbean-definition-peer-review/.

Fresh online recovery on 30 September 2026 found the current IPPC publication page for ISPM 32 (page publication date 28 July 2025) and the Russian official version it presently links. Read section 2 Category 1 and Appendix 2 printed page 32-18: tea (Чай) is expressly listed as a Category 1 example. Appendix 2 is marked reference-only and not prescriptive. The linked text is older (publication history through 2013); the 2025 webpage date is not represented as a new substantive rule.

Applied the recovered commodity example to domestic law, not membership alone: article 1(1)(bb) has a risk-qualified processed-product definition, and article 1(2) expressly gives IPPC/SPS term meanings and associated standards/guidelines priority. Article 6 document duties and article 14 postal interception use those defined categories. This supplies a defensible combined-source inference that commercially manufactured steamed/dried plain Camellia tea is Category 1 and outside the controlled scope; the prior missing-classification gap is superseded.

Re-read the complete 2020 Act articles 1–2 and 5–9 plus the actual August 2026 procedure notice. Article 6(3)’s limited frozen-fruit/vegetable certificate exception does not itself regulate every other manufactured food. The 2026 notice restates articles 5–8 for plants and plant products without a new manufactured-tea definition. Current ministry media-index search recovered that same 2026 notice, with no tea-specific contrary condition. No speculative unpublished waiver is assumed.

Retained prior independent food/trade review: the 2003 trade Negative List’s plant certificate row omits chapter 9; 2006 amendment concerns other goods; current 2026 Food Act remains a pending bill. Business-only registration rules were not applied to this private postal recipient. Combined with the now-resolved plant scope, no separate special-document barrier has been established.
permitFreeReason: Legal-scope inference: domestic article 1(2) incorporates the applicable IPPC/SPS term meanings and associated standards/guidelines; the current-linked ISPM 32 tea example resolves the manufactured-product risk threshold in article 1(1)(bb) for the stated processed retail sencha. No phytosanitary permit/certificate route under articles 5–8 is needed for a product outside that scope. This is not reliance on IPPC membership alone, nor a claim that the reference-only Appendix itself overrides a specific national restriction.
paperworkType: None identified for the stated personal manufactured-tea parcel; ordinary postal/customs declaration and arrival inspection remain.
requiredDocument: Ordinary postal/customs declaration only under the reviewed plant/food rules; no phytosanitary permit or certificate on the stated scope inference.
